INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE 1
Amici curiae are non-profit, non-partisan, public
interest organizations that advocate for and serve
transgender youth throughout the State of Washington.
These organizations are experts on the legal, social, and
economic barriers faced by transgender youth. Amici
are deeply invested in ensuring dignity and safety for all
gender-diverse and transgender people, especially youth.
Lavender Rights Project (LRP) is a Black Trans-led
non-profit organization located in Seattle, Washington.
LRP advances gender self-determination, collective
safety, and community-rooted systems of care through
impacting the criminalization system, housing justice,
and policy advocacy. LRP serves and is guided by
Black, Indigenous, and gender-diverse communities in
Washington. Through legal intervention, community
mobilization, and permanent supportive housing, LRP
advocates for Black and gender-diverse communities by
centering those most marginalized.
Legal Voice’s mission is to advance gender justice in
the Northwest, which includes supporting the autonomy
of transgender youth. In pursuit of its mission, Legal
Voice uses a combination of litigation, policy advocacy,
and community education to advance economic justice,
eradicate gender discrimination, ensure access to health
care, protect reproductive freedom, and end gender-based

building, community and lawmaker issue education,
policy change, and leadership development. Its mission is
to protect, restore, and expand every person’s right and
ability to access the full range of affordable, quality, and
unbiased abortion, sexual, and reproductive health care
information and services through movement-building,
community education, and grassroots advocacy.
QLaw Foundation of Washington (“QLaw”) promotes
the dignity and respect of 2SLGBTQIA+ individuals,
families, and communities in Washington. QLaw
executes its mission by providing legal services to
2SLGBTQIA+ communities through free legal clinics,
direct representation, impact litigation, and policy
advocacy. For eighteen years, QLaw has engaged in
extensive litigation, appellate work, and amicus support
in the Western District of Washington, the Ninth Circuit,
and the United States Supreme Court, as well as in
Washington State courts. Serving over 100 clients every
year, QLaw has extensive understanding of the issues

3

United Territories of Pacific Islanders Alliance

LGBTQIA+ non-profit organization based in Kent,

to LGBTQIA+ individuals and other underserved

Spectrum Center Spokane (“Spectrum”) is an

that uplifts the 2SLGBTQIA+ community in Eastern
Washington and North Idaho. Spectrum advances equity
through community care, advocacy, and education, with
the vision that 2SLGBTQIA+ individuals thrive in

been supporting transgender people and their families
since 2008. It runs parent support groups and special
topics groups. All of its programs are available online
and available to families throughout the United States,
including Washington.
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
In 2023, the Washington State Legislature passed
Engrossed Substitute Senate Bill (ESSB) 5599 to
address the crisis of transgender youth homelessness.

4
ESSB 5599, 68th Leg., Reg. Sess. (Wash. 2023), enacted
as 2023 Wash. Sess. Laws, ch. 408 (amending Wash.
Rev. Code § 13.32A.082). The bill amended the Family
Reconciliation Act, requiring the Department of Children,
Youth, and Families (DCYF) to notify parents and offer
voluntary family reunification and mental health services
to youth and their families, if a young person appears
at a homeless shelter and is seeking gender-affirming
treatment. Id. Petitioners are parents who fear a highlyattenuated chain of “mights”—that their children might
be transgender, might run away, might fin d s pace a t a
homeless shelter, and then might somehow access genderaffirming treatment against the parents’ wishes, despite
laws requiring parental consent for medical care.
The Ninth Circuit correctly held that Petitioners do
not have standing in this case. Pet.App.4a–5a. The object
of ESSB 5599 is protecting and stabilizing youth in crisis,
not curtailing the rights of parents. This is demonstrated
through the plain meaning of the statute and the
legislative record, as well as the needs and interests of
youth. Petitioners are unable to show injury in fact because
their hypothetical chain of events is based on fallacies and
incorrect assumptions. They ignore the fact that accessing
gender-affirming care in Washington is a thoughtful,
lengthy process that requires parental involvement at
various stages. Most importantly, parenting a transgender
child is not itself an injury or harm. ESSB 5599 gives
both parents and children an opportunity to learn about
optional supportive services and ultimately recommit to
an enriching relationship.
The Court should affirm the lower courts and its own
precedent by holding that Petitioners lack standing.

5
ARGUMENT
I.  PETITIONERS FAIL TO SHOW INJURY AND
ARE NOT THE OBJECTS OF THE FAMILY
RECONCILIATION ACT
To establish standing, Petitioners must demonstrate
that they have suffered an injury in fact. Clapper v.
Amnesty Int’l USA, 568 U.S. 398, 409 (2013). This requires
proof of a “concrete, particularized” injury that is “actual
or imminent.” Id. (citation modified). Petitioners have
failed to make such a showing, pointing to only their selfimposed parenting choices and attenuated, improbable,
hypothetical future harms, rather than actual injuries.
To avoid the requirement of actual or imminent harm,
Petitioners allege they are the “objects of the laws here.”
Pet’rs’ Br. at 24. Even if this were true, Petitioners must
still demonstrate injury, causation, and redressability. See
Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife , 504 U.S. 555, 560–61 (1992).
They cannot, as they claim, establish standing merely
from being the objects of the law. Pet’rs’ Br. at 21–22.
And moreover, Petitioners fail to even demonstrate that
they are the objects of the law. The objects of the Family
Reconciliation Act amendments are young people and the
shelters and agencies who serve them.
A.  The Purpose of the Family Reconciliation
Act Amendments is to Protect and Stabilize
Youth and to Promote Healthy Parent-Child
Relationships
The Washington State Legislature enacted the
Family Reconciliation Act and its amendments to protect
and stabilize youth who are at risk of homelessness. Wash.
Rev. Code § 13.32A.010; 2023 Wash. Sess. Laws ch. 408,

6
§ 1. 2 The Family Reconciliation Act amendments were
not enacted to target parents, and they do not do so. See
Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082 (2023). The statute’s plain
language, its legislative history, and the role of DCYF in
supporting youth in Washington demonstrate that the true
object of the law is young people and their safety.
The Court has long held that if a statute’s meaning is
plain and clear, that meaning must be enforced regardless
of other considerations. E.g., United States v. Ron Pair
Enters., Inc., 489 U.S. 235, 241 (1989) (“[W]here . . . the
statute’s language is plain, ‘the sole function of the
courts is to enforce it according to its terms.’” (quoting
Caminetti v. United States , 242 U.S. 470, 485 (1917)).
The plain language of ESSB 5599 explicitly relates to
the protection and support of youth in crisis, including
outlining alternative notice procedures. See 2023 Wash.
Sess. Laws, ch. 408, § 1 (stating that “the legislature
intends to remove barriers to accessing temporary,
licensed shelter accommodations for youth seeking
certain protected health care services”); Wash. Rev. Code
§ 13.32A.082(1)(b)(i) (requiring shelters to notify DCYF

§ 13.32A.082(3) (2023).

7

changes to parental rights.
The statute’s legislative history also makes clear that
the object of the law is the protection and stabilization
of unhoused youth. For example, Senator Claire Wilson
described the bill as centered on “crisis stabilization for
young people so they don’t spiral out of control and that
we can connect with them and provide them services and
supports that they need.” Executive Session on SB 5599

at 19:37–19:46 (Wash. Feb. 14, 2023), https://tvw.org/video/
senate-human-services-2023021335 . Senator Joe Nguyen
said it simply: “This is about housing and about shelter.”
Id. at 17:03–17:05. During debate on the House Floor,
Representative Julio Cortes explained that the statute’s
focus is youth safety: “The purpose of this bill is to help
to eliminate the chilling impact parent notifications can
sometimes have . . . this bill is intended . . . to ensure that
these youth have access to safe housing. From there we
will be able to work on family reconciliation services.”
House Floor Debate on ESSB 5599, 68th Leg., Reg. Sess.
at 1:54:44–1:55:13 (Wash. Apr. 12, 2023), https://tvw.org/
video/house-floor-debate-april-12-2023041141/ .
Lawmakers were concerned that some youth could
leave the safety of youth shelters for the streets if parents
were immediately notified of their whereabouts. See, e.g.,
id. at 2:32:07–2:33:45. ESSB 5599 allows a brief pause and
the involvement of DCYF , to encourage youth to remain
in shelters while accessing family reconciliation services.
Lawmakers in both chambers consistently echoed this
sentiment: the focus of this bill was to support and protect
youth, not to interfere with or impact parental rights.

8
DCYF is the state agency focusing on “prevention
and better outcomes for children, youth, and families.” 3
Prior to the passage of ESSB 5599, DCYF already
offered optional reconciliation services to all families who
requested them in order to “bring the youth and family
together” with the goal of “preserv[ing], strengthen[ing],
and reconcil[ing] families[.]”4 DCYF has long recognized
the important role parents or guardians play in youth
development and safety.5 Parents or children may request
family reconciliation services as an additional support
while navigating complex relationships and serious
conflict. These voluntary services include referrals for
substance abuse treatment or counseling, referrals for
mental health services, and short-term family intervention
services. 6 The goal of family reconciliation services is

B.  Complex Family Dynamics Are Not Analogous
to Economic Inferences and Do Not
Demonstrate That Parents Are Objects of the
Law
Though the object of ESSB 5599 is to support youth
and families, Petitioners insist that they are objects of the
law. They cite cases where courts have found standing for
non-regulated entities due to interference with economic
relationships. Pet’rs’ Br. at 22–23, 28 (citing Diamond
Alt. Energy v. EPA , 606 U.S. 100, 114 (2025) and Pierce
v. Soc’y of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510, 535–36 (1925)). But these
cases are not analogous to the complex questions of family
dynamics, youth interests, and parenting choices at issue
here. For example, in Diamond Alternative Energy , the
Court found standing for fuel producers where third-party
automakers were likely to react to government regulation
and decrease demand for fuel, based on “commonsense
economic principles” and “economic inferences about
the operation of the automobile market[.]” 606 U.S. at
116, 120. These economic principles made third-party
behavior “predictable,” thereby allowing the Court to
infer downstream economic injury to fuel producers. Id.
at 116 –17.
Similarly, in Pierce, plaintiff schools had standing to
challenge a law prohibiting parents from enrolling their
children because the challenged law limited the schools’
customer base. 268 U.S. at 536. The Court recognized
that “enforcement of the statute would seriously impair,

10
perhaps destroy, the profitable features of [plaintiff
schools]’ business and greatly diminish the value of their
property.” Id. at 531. These direct economic harms sufficed
to show that “[t]he injury to appellees was present and
very real, not a mere possibility in the remote future.”
Id. at 536.
No such economic principles apply to the complex
question of how a young person feels at home and where
they might turn for safety and support. There is no
“predictable” pattern of behavior akin to “commonsense
economic principles” that permits an inference of injury.
Diamond Alt. Energy , 606 U.S. at 116. The motivations
and choices of parents and children in how they behave
vary immensely. Family dynamics are unique and fluid.
For example, as discussed in Section III, infra, many
parents are unsure of how to respond to and support
their LGBTQ+ children, but their perspectives and
approaches evolve over time. Research shows that
certain interventions, like providing information and
resources to parents of LGBTQ+ kids, can support
children and strengthen families.7 A wide range of factors
beyond a young person’s parents can affect how the
young person navigates their gender identity and finds
emotional support. 8 Unlike the economic relationships

or do not have at home and elsewhere, and whether they

C.  At-Risk Youth Are the True Object of the Law
Petitioners’ standing, and their assertions about
parental rights, cannot be analyzed in a vacuum. The
interests of the Petitioners’ children matter, too, and
must be considered as part of the calculus in assessing
any argument that there has been an infringement of the
parents’ rights. It is well-established that young people
have their own rights separate from those of their parents,
including rights to speak their minds, to receive education,
and to access health care. See, e.g., Tinker v. Des Moines
Indep. Cmty. Sch. Dist. , 393 U.S. 503, 505–06 (1969);
Pierce, 268 U.S. at 535; Carey v. Population Servs., Int’l,
431 U.S. 678, 693 (1977). In the seminal case of Parham v.
J.R., the Court upheld a statute that allowed a child’s parent
or guardian to initiate the child’s voluntary admission to a
psychiatric hospital, provided that “some kind of inquiry
[is] made by a ‘neutral factfinder’ to determine whether
the statutory requirements for admission are satisfied.”
442 U.S. 584, 606 (1979). But the Court also recognized
youth’s independent constitutional rights and emphasized
that youth’s interests in bodily autonomy and freedom
from restraint must be respected. Id. at 600–01, 606–07.
Youth in Washington deserve access to shelter, mental
school connectedness, community involvement, personal resilience,
self-esteem, and access to supportive friends, family and community).

12
health care, and services supporting reunification with
their families.
Recognizing the importance of youth health and
safety, ESSB 5599 addresses the needs of youth who are
in crisis and have left home by ensuring they have a place
to stay and receive referrals for needed services. See
Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082(1)–(3). These young people
face serious safety risks if they are on the streets, and
they may have significant mental health needs. Access to
mental health care is especially important for transgender
youth and youth experiencing gender dysphoria. Research
shows that a disproportionate number of transgender
young people face serious mental health challenges,
often due to stigma and lack of support. 9 In 2024, forty
percent of transgender and nonbinary youth seriously
considered attempting suicide.10 These same youth report
increased rates of depression and anxiety compared to
their cisgender peers, 11 making access to mental health
care essential to their wellbeing and survival. The object of
ESSB 5599 is to make sure these youth are sheltered and
stabilized, while simultaneously facilitating reunification
with their parents.

II.  THE PROCESS OF YOUTH ACCESSING
GENDER-AFFIRMING CARE IN WASHINGTON
STATE IS THOUGHTFULLY CONSIDERED AND
INVOLVES P ARENTS
Petitioners lack standing because their claims rely on a
fundamental misunderstanding of how young people access
health care and gender-affirming care in Washington.
Their theories of standing are premised on the belief
that their children may run away, find a bed at a youth
shelter, and ultimately access gender-affirming treatment
without their consent. See Pet’rs’ Br. at 17. That belief is
unsupported by the law and the reality of accessing genderaffirming medical treatment in Washington. Therefore,
the Petitioners do not have an injury that is “concrete,
particularized, and actual or imminent” in this case.
Clapper, 568 U.S. at 409 (citation modified).
In Washington, the process of accessing genderaffirming treatment is deliberate, lengthy, and requires
parental involvement. Gender-affirming medical
treatment requires parental consent for patients under
eighteen.12 Starting gender-affirming medical treatment
is dependent on a diagnosis of gender dysphoria by a
mental health provider or physician, after which a team
of medical providers work with a patient and their family
to create an individualized care plan. 13 This care begins

III. PARENTING A TRANSGENDER CHILD IS NOT
AN INJURY OR HARM
Petitioners’ standing argument hinges on the
occurrence of a “highly attenuated chain of possibilities,”
Clapper, 568 U.S. at 410, which Petitioners assert exposes
them to the “threat” of injury, Pet’rs’ Br. at 21. The
threatened injury that Petitioners seek to avoid is being
forced to parent in a certain way. Id. But ESSB 5599 does
not require Petitioners to parent in a particular way. While
some parents may find it challenging to have children who
identify differently from how their parents raised them,
that itself does not rise to the level of a constitutional
harm. Many parents of transgender children have an
evolving perspective on how to parent their children, and
ultimately, the relationship between a supportive parent
and their child can be a source of strength and positive
outcomes for both. As demonstrated in their published
accounts, many parents of transgender children celebrate
and take pride in parenting them.
A.  Parents Describe Parenting Their Transgender
Children as Positive and Rewarding
In published accounts, parents describe their
commitment to affirm and support their transgender
child:
I’m writing this essay while looking at two
pictures of the same person. One is an old

my wonderful boy, now with short hair, the
same big, brown eyes, wearing his signature
leather jacket and looking into the camera with
confidence and a broad grin—someone I would
not have missed knowing for anything in the

Even parents who forthrightly acknowledge their
initial misgivings recount celebrating the joy they have
experienced while witnessing and participating in the
growth of their child, who blossoms with the benefit of
parental support:
This child, while wonderful and exuberant, and
happy beyond anything I’d ever seen before, was

could never tell me any toy that she wanted,
suddenly had a list a mile long. I felt horrible
that I’d never bothered to take her down the
aisles of pink and purple. I never would have
said my child had been unhappy until I saw who
she was becoming. 17

B.  Transgender Youth and Youth Experiencing
Gender Dysphoria Benefit from Parental
Support
Just as parents describe growth and joy in parenting
transgender children, transgender youth and youth
experiencing gender dysphoria benefit from having
understanding parents. In her account of parenting her
adolescent daughter, Jamie Bruesehoff recalls realizing
that “youth do not struggle because there is something

The 2022 U.S. Transgender Survey, which analyzed

CONCLUSION
The Ninth Circuit correctly determined that
Petitioners lacked standing to challenge the laws at
issue here. Petitioners are unable to articulate concrete,
particularized injuries as required under the longstanding
precedent of this Court. The Petitioners are not the
targets of ESSB 5599—runaway youth are. The Court
should affirm the lower courts.
